claim: The genetic basis of most traits is highly polygenic and dominated by non-coding alleles.
source: The genetic basis of most traits is highly polygenic and dominated by non-coding alleles.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of complex trait genetics.

claim: It is widely assumed that non-coding alleles exert small regulatory effects on the expression of cis-linked genes.
source: It is widely assumed that such alleles exert small regulatory effects on the expression of cis-linked genes.
evidence: This describes a prevailing assumption in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: 220 gene–trait pairs were identified in which protein-coding variants influence a complex trait or its Mendelian cognate.
source: To better distinguish between these possibilities, we identified 220 gene–trait pairs in which protein-coding variants influence a complex trait or its Mendelian cognate.
evidence: This is supported by the data collection and analysis described in the manuscript, including Table 1 and references to Backman et al., 2021.

claim: Expression quantitative trait loci are present near most GWAS associations.
source: Despite the presence of expression quantitative trait loci near most GWAS associations, by applying a gene-based approach we found limited evidence that the baseline expression of trait-related genes explains GWAS associations
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis showing 91.1% of genes near GWAS peaks had eQTLs.

claim: Only 8% of putatively causative genes were implicated by colocalization methods.
source: by applying a gene-based approach we found limited evidence that the baseline expression of trait-related genes explains GWAS associations, whether using colocalization methods (8% of genes implicated)
evidence: This is directly supported by the colocalization analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only 2% of putatively causative genes were implicated by transcription-wide association studies.
source: transcription-wide association (2% of genes implicated)
evidence: This is directly supported by the TWAS analysis results when restricted to relevant tissues.

claim: Only 4% of putatively causative genes were implicated by a combination of regulatory annotations and distance.
source: or a combination of regulatory annotations and distance (4% of genes implicated)
evidence: This is supported by the chromatin analysis results using activity-by-distance scores.

claim: These results contradict the hypothesis that most complex trait-associated variants coincide with homeostatic expression QTLs.
source: These results contradict the hypothesis that most complex trait-associated variants coincide with homeostatic expression QTLs, suggesting that better models are needed.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low rates of colocalization and TWAS findings.

claim: The 'mystery of missing heritability' refers to the inability of common and rare variants to explain a large fraction of trait heritability.
source: the 'mystery of missing heritability,' in which no combination of common and rare variants can explain a large fraction of trait heritability (Manolio et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manolio et al., 2009.

claim: Most human traits exhibit unexpectedly high polygenicity with very small effect sizes for individual variants.
source: Further work has revealed unexpectedly high polygenicity for most human traits and very small effect sizes for individual variants.
evidence: This represents established knowledge from the field of complex trait genetics.

claim: A large fraction of heritability resides in regions with gene regulatory potential, predominantly tissue-specific accessible chromatin and enhancer elements.
source: Enrichment analyses have demonstrated that a large fraction of heritability resides in regions with gene regulatory potential, predominantly tissue-specific accessible chromatin and enhancer elements, suggesting that trait-associated variants influence gene regulation (Maurano et al., 2012; Trynka et al., 2013; Gusev et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Maurano et al., 2012; Trynka et al., 2013; Gusev et al., 2014).

claim: Genes in trait-associated loci are more likely to have genetic variants that affect their expression levels (eQTLs).
source: Furthermore, genes in trait-associated loci are more likely to have genetic variants that affect their expression levels (expression quantitative trait loci, or eQTLs)
evidence: This represents established knowledge from eQTL studies.

claim: Variants with the strongest trait associations are more likely to be associated with transcript abundance of at least one proximal gene.
source: and the variants with the strongest trait associations are more likely also to be associated with transcript abundance of at least one proximal gene (Nicolae et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nicolae et al., 2010.

claim: A model has emerged in which most trait-associated variants influence proximal gene regulation.
source: Thus, a model has emerged in which most trait-associated variants influence proximal gene regulation.
evidence: This describes the prevailing model in the field based on accumulated evidence.

claim: The unembellished model in which GWAS peaks are mediated by effects on homeostatic expression assayed in tissue samples is the exception rather than the rule.
source: Here we argue that this unembellished model—in which genome-wide association study (GWAS) peaks are mediated by the effects on the homeostatic expression assayed in tissue samples—is the exception rather than the rule.
evidence: This is the main argument of the paper, inferred from the data presented.

claim: There is a difference between spatial distributions of eQTLs and GWAS peaks, with eQTLs dramatically enriched in close proximity to genes while GWAS peaks are usually farther away.
source: One challenge is the difference between spatial distributions of eQTLs, which are dramatically enriched in close proximity to genes, and GWAS peaks, which are usually farther away (Stranger et al., 2007; Farh et al., 2015; Mostafavi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Stranger et al., 2007; Farh et al., 2015; Mostafavi et al., 2022).

claim: Expression levels mediate a minority of complex trait heritability.
source: Another is that expression levels mediate a minority of complex trait heritability (Yao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yao et al., 2020.

claim: Only 5–40% of trait associations colocalize with eQTLs across studies.
source: If the model is correct, most trait associations should also be eQTLs, but across studies, only 5–40% of trait associations colocalize with eQTLs (Giambartolomei et al., 2014; Chun et al., 2017; Giambartolomei et al., 2018; Hormozdiari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple colocalization studies.

claim: Genes whose coding variants can cause detectable phenotypic change are expected to be influenced by variants of small effect.
source: For genes whose coding variants can cause detectable phenotypic change, the strong expectation is that a variant of small effect influences the gene identified by its rare coding variants.
evidence: This is based on biological reasoning and inference from the relationship between Mendelian and complex traits.

claim: APOE and LDLR are both low-density lipoprotein receptor genes.
source: As an example, APOE and LDLR are both low-density lipoprotein receptor genes (Schneider et al., 1981; Goldstein and Brown, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schneider et al., 1981 and Goldstein and Brown, 1973.

claim: Coding variants in APOE and LDLR can lead to the Mendelian disorder familial hypercholesterolemia.
source: Coding variants in APOE and LDLR can lead to the Mendelian disorder familial hypercholesterolemia (Goldstein and Brown, 1973; Cenarro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldstein and Brown, 1973 and Cenarro et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of APOE and LDLR in animal models reduces cholesterol levels.
source: Even in the absence of a Mendelian coding variant, experiments in animal models have found that the overexpression of these genes reduces cholesterol levels (Shimano et al., 1992a; Shimano et al., 1992b; Kawashiri et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies in animal models.

claim: GWAS on human subjects have found significant associations near APOE and LDLR.
source: GWAS on human subjects have found significant associations near APOE and LDLR
evidence: This is based on established GWAS findings.

claim: The analysis included four common diseases: type II diabetes, ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease, and breast cancer.
source: Our selection included four common diseases: type II diabetes (T2D) (Mahajan et al., 2018), where early-onset familial forms are caused by rare coding mutations (insulin-independent MODY; neonatal diabetes; maternally inherited diabetes and deafness; familial partial lipodystrophy); ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn disease (CD) (Liu et al., 2015; Goyette et al., 2015), which have Mendelian pediatric forms characterized by severity of presentation; and breast cancer (BC) (Zhang et al., 2020), where germline coding mutations (e.g., BRCA1) or somatic tissue (e.g., PIK3CA) are sufficient for disease.
evidence: This describes the study design and data sources used.

claim: The analysis included three quantitative traits: low- and high-density lipoprotein levels and height.
source: We also chose three quantitative traits: low- and high-density lipoprotein levels (LDL and HDL); and height.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The analysis included 220 unique gene-trait pairs between known Mendelian genes and those from Backman et al., 2021.
source: Between known Mendelian genes and those from Backman et al., 2021, our analysis included 220 unique gene-trait pairs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data collection described and shown in Figure 1.

claim: 147 out of 220 genes (67%) fell within 1 Mb of a GWAS locus for the cognate complex trait.
source: Of our 220 genes, 147 (67%) fell within 1 Mb of a GWAS locus for the cognate complex trait, over three times as many as the 43 predicted by a random null model (95% confidence interval: 31.5–54.5).
evidence: This is directly supported by the enrichment analysis results.

claim: The enrichment of putatively causative genes near GWAS peaks is over three times higher than predicted by a random null model.
source: Of our 220 genes, 147 (67%) fell within 1 Mb of a GWAS locus for the cognate complex trait, over three times as many as the 43 predicted by a random null model (95% confidence interval: 31.5–54.5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison to a null model.

claim: At a distance of 100 kb, 104 putatively causative genes (47%) were found near GWAS peaks, while the null model predicts only 11.
source: At a distance of 100 kb, we find 104 putatively causative genes (47%), though the null model predicts only 11 (95% CI 4.5–17.0), an order-of-magnitude enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment of putatively causative genes near GWAS peaks represents an order-of-magnitude enrichment at 100 kb distance.
source: At a distance of 100 kb, we find 104 putatively causative genes (47%), though the null model predicts only 11 (95% CI 4.5–17.0), an order-of-magnitude enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing observed to expected values.

claim: 134 out of 147 genes (91.1%) near GWAS peaks had an eQTL in at least one relevant tissue at FDR Q < 0.05.
source: Controlling for the number of tests we conducted, 134 (91.1%) of these genes had an eQTL in at least one relevant tissue at a false discovery rate (FDR) of Q < 0.05 ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is directly supported by the eQTL detection analysis.

claim: Only 7 genes out of 147 (4.8%) showed colocalization of trait and eQTL association using coloc.
source: We found support for the colocalization of trait and eQTL association for only 7 genes out of 147 (4.8%) for coloc
evidence: This is directly supported by the colocalization analysis results.

claim: Only 10 genes out of 147 (6.8%) showed colocalization of trait and eQTL association using JLIM.
evidence: This is directly supported by the colocalization analysis results.

claim: Only 8 genes out of 147 (5.4%) showed colocalization of trait and eQTL association using eCAVIAR.
source: and 8/147 (5.4%) for eCAVIAR
evidence: This is directly supported by the colocalization analysis results.

claim: Accounting for overlap, only 18 out of 220 putatively causative genes (8.2%) showed colocalization.
source: Accounting for overlap, this represents only 18/220 putatively causative genes (8.2%) or 18/147 (12.2%) putatively causative genes near GWAS peaks
evidence: This is directly supported by the combined colocalization analysis results.

claim: Prior estimates suggest 25–40% of GWAS associations colocalize with eQTLs.
source: We note that prior estimates of the fraction of GWAS associations colocalizing with eQTLs (25–40%; Giambartolomei et al., 2014; Chun et al., 2017; Hormozdiari et al., 2016; Wen et al., 2017) do not directly evaluate the ability to find causative genes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: MASH increased the number of GWAS-eQTL colocalizations across all genes by 26% (from 389 to 489).
source: Rerunning coloc with these modified statistics increased the number of GWAS-eQTL colocalizations across all genes by 26% (from 389 to 489).
evidence: This is directly supported by the MASH analysis results.

claim: The 100 new colocalizations identified by MASH identified only four additional putatively causative genes.
source: However, the 100 new colocalizations identified only four additional putatively causative genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the MASH analysis results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tissue-type selection was not the limiting factor in the analysis.
source: These results indicate that tissue-type selection was not the limiting factor in our analysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the MASH results showing minimal improvement in identifying putatively causative genes.

claim: FUSION TWAS identified putatively causative genes as likely tied to the GWAS peak in 66 out of 220 loci (30%).
source: FUSION included our putatively causative genes in the set identified as likely relevant to the GWAS peak in 66/220 loci (30%).
evidence: This is directly supported by the TWAS analysis results.

claim: Only 4 out of 220 genes (1.8%) were identified by FUSION when restricted to relevant tissues.
source: However, only 4/220 (1.8%) genes were identified by FUSION when we restricted the analysis to relevant tissues.
evidence: This is directly supported by the tissue-restricted TWAS analysis results.

claim: For 37 genes in the Mendelian subset, at least one high-confidence fine-mapped variant (PIP > 0.7) was identified within 100 kb of the transcription start site.
source: For 37 of these genes, we identified at least one high-confidence fine-mapped variant (defined as a variant with posterior inclusion probability, or PIP, greater than 0.7) within 100 kb of the transcription start site.
evidence: This is directly supported by the fine-mapping analysis using SuSiE.

claim: 32 out of 37 genes (86%) have a fine-mapped variant within a candidate regulatory region across all tissue types examined.
source: As many as 32/37 (86%) genes identified this way have a fine-mapped variants within a candidate regulatory region across all the tissue types examined
evidence: This is directly supported by the functional genomic annotation analysis.

claim: 25 out of 37 genes (68%) have a fine-mapped variant within a candidate regulatory region when restricting to trait-relevant tissues.
source: or 25/37 (68%) when restricting to trait-relevant tissues (Figure 2); (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is directly supported by the tissue-restricted functional genomic annotation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only 5 out of 25 loci (20%) with fine-mapped variants in regulatory regions demonstrably correspond to expression effects in eQTL analysis.
source: Despite this strong evidence that these GWAS associations arise from effects on regulatory DNA, only 5/25 loci (20%) demonstrably correspond to expression effects in our eQTL analysis.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparing the regulatory annotation results with eQTL colocalization results.

claim: Using activity-by-distance scores, 5 out of 37 genes (14%) from the Mendelian subset were implicated.
source: Taking each locus's feature with the highest ABD score, we implicate 5/37 (14%) of our Mendelian subset of genes.
evidence: This is directly supported by the ABD score analysis.

claim: The results are strongly consistent with the idea that complex traits are governed by non-coding genetic variants whose effects on phenotype are mediated by their contribution to the regulation of nearby genes.
source: Overall, our results are strongly consistent with the idea that complex traits are governed by non-coding genetic variants whose effects on phenotype are mediated by their contribution to the regulation of nearby genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of putatively causative genes near GWAS peaks and the presence of regulatory features.

claim: The results are inconsistent with a model that effects on gene regulation arise from genetic influences on baseline gene expression captured by eQTLs.
source: However, these same results are inconsistent with a model that such effects on gene regulation arise from the genetic influences on baseline gene expression that are captured by eQTLs.
evidence: This is inferred from the low rates of colocalization between GWAS peaks and eQTLs for putatively causative genes.

claim: The enrichment of putatively causative genes near GWAS peaks supports their role in complex traits.
source: The enrichment of putatively causative genes—selected based on existing biological knowledge—near GWAS peaks supports their role in complex traits.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment analysis results.

claim: The enrichment of fine-mapped GWAS variants in likely regulatory regions supports the general model of GWAS associations arising from effects on gene regulation.
source: Additionally, the enrichment of fine-mapped GWAS variants in likely regulatory regions marked by DHS and other chromatin features lends support to the general model of GWAS associations arising from effects on gene regulation and expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional genomic annotation analysis results.

claim: The inability of varied statistical methods to connect GWAS associations and expression argues against the idea that causative GWAS variants exert their effects via homeostatic or blended effects on gene expression captured by bulk-tissue eQTLs.
source: However, the inability of varied statistical methods to connect GWAS associations and expression argues against the idea that the causative GWAS variants exert their effects via the homeostatic or blended effects on gene expression that are captured by bulk-tissue eQTLs of the sort discovered by broad expression-data collection projects.
evidence: This is inferred from the low success rates of colocalization and TWAS methods.

claim: Non-expression-mediated mechanisms are not applicable as an explanation for the negative results in the context examined.
source: As a result, we conclude that a number of explanations often considered when evaluating expression-based variant-to-gene methods are not applicable in the context we examined. These include (i) non-expression-mediated mechanisms
evidence: This is inferred from the study design and results, particularly the enrichment of regulatory features.

claim: Lack of statistical power for GWAS is not applicable as an explanation for the negative results in the context examined.
source: These include (i) non-expression-mediated mechanisms, (ii) lack of statistical power for GWAS
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that 67% of genes were near GWAS peaks, indicating sufficient GWAS power.

claim: The absence of eQTLs for relevant genes is not applicable as an explanation for the negative results in the context examined.
source: These include (i) non-expression-mediated mechanisms, (ii) lack of statistical power for GWAS, (iii) the absence of eQTLs for relevant genes
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that 91.1% of genes near GWAS peaks had eQTLs.

claim: Underpowered methods for linking expression to GWAS are not applicable as an explanation for the negative results in the context examined.
source: These include (i) non-expression-mediated mechanisms, (ii) lack of statistical power for GWAS, (iii) the absence of eQTLs for relevant genes, (iv) and underpowered methods for linking expression to GWAS (Table 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the use of multiple well-powered methods and the consistency of negative results.

claim: There remains to be discovered a major component connecting variants to gene expression, termed 'missing regulation.'
source: Our results suggest that there remains to be discovered a major component connecting variants to gene expression, which we term 'missing regulation.'
evidence: This is inferred from the gap between GWAS associations and eQTL colocalization.

claim: The 'missing regulation' could be exposed by considering context-dependent gene expression confined to particular refined cell types or anatomical partitions.
source: We propose that this currently lacking component could be exposed by considering more nuanced experimental and analytical models of gene expression. One likely model involves context-dependent gene expression—expression whose relevant effects are confined to (i) particular refined cell types or anatomical partitions
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the negative results and known limitations of bulk tissue analysis.

claim: The 'missing regulation' could be exposed by considering context-dependent gene expression confined to cell states such as responses to perturbations.
source: or (ii) cell states such as responses to perturbations, whether exogenous (e.g., environmental change) or endogenous (e.g., cell differentiation)
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the negative results and known limitations of homeostatic expression analysis.

claim: A complementary model may incorporate heterogeneity of gene expression or the variance of expression across relatively short time scales.
source: A complementary model may incorporate heterogeneity of gene expression or the variance of expression across relatively short time scales.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for alternative models of gene regulation.

claim: Models may depend on or be augmented by thresholding or buffering of variant effects, which may produce changes in gene expression with nonlinear effects on phenotype.
source: These models and others may depend on or be augmented by thresholding or buffering of variant effects, which may produce changes in gene expression with nonlinear effects on phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for mechanisms that could explain the disconnect between eQTLs and phenotypes.

claim: Low rates of positive findings for expression-based variant-to-gene methods have constrained the discovery of genes contributing to complex traits.
source: One long-standing goal of GWAS has been to discover genes contributing to complex traits (Manolio et al., 2009; Farh et al., 2015), but low rates of positive findings for expression-based variant-to-gene methods have constrained this possibility (Chun et al., 2017; Baird et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting the challenges in gene discovery.

claim: The challenges in linking GWAS to genes have limited the benefit of GWAS and expression data for disease-gene mapping and drug discovery.
source: Among other challenges, this has limited the benefit of GWAS and expression data for disease-gene mapping and drug discovery (Baird et al., 2021; Umans et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on the applications of GWAS.

claim: If the most relevant models depend on effects not observable in homeostatic eQTL mapping, the field may need to prioritize other biological contexts and forms of expression data.
source: If the most relevant models are shown to depend on effects not observable in homeostatic eQTL mapping, the field may need to consider prioritizing other biological contexts and forms of expression data.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: 128 genes harboring large-effect-size coding variants were selected by manual literature search for one of seven phenotypes.
source: By manual literature search, we selected 128 genes harboring large-effect-size coding variants for one of the seven phenotypes (Table 1; specifically, we selected 128 gene–trait pairs, representing 121 unique genes).
evidence: This describes the methodology for gene selection.

claim: For breast cancer, genes were selected using the MutPanning method.
source: and, for breast cancer, using the MutPanning method (Dietlein et al., 2020)
evidence: This describes the methodology for breast cancer gene selection, supported by citation.

claim: The inclusion of genes from Backman et al. ensures that results are not dependent on an undetected bias in gene selection.
source: The inclusion of genes from Backman et al. ensures that our results are not dependent on an undetected bias in our selection.
evidence: This explains the rationale for including an independent gene set.

claim: GWAS sample sizes are large enough to detect low-frequency coding variants used to select some of the genes.
source: Because GWAS sample sizes are large enough to detect the low-frequency coding variants used to select some of our genes, it is possible that a coding variant would distort the association signal of nearby eQTLs.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GWAS power and study design considerations.

claim: The effects of coding variants on GWAS were removed to minimize the concern that coding variants would distort the association signal of nearby eQTLs.
source: To minimize this concern, we removed the effects of coding variants on GWAS.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to address a potential confound.

claim: For height, LDL cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol, GWAS were performed using genotypic and phenotypic data from the UK Biobank.
source: For height, LDL cholesterol, and HDL cholesterol, GWAS were performed using genotypic and phenotypic data from the UKBB.
evidence: This describes the data sources and methods used for GWAS.

claim: The GWAS sample was restricted to 337K unrelated individuals with genetically determined British ancestry to avoid confounding.
source: In order to avoid confounding, we restricted our sample to the 337K unrelated individuals with genetically determined British ancestry identified by Bycroft et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes the sample selection criteria, supported by citation.

claim: For breast cancer, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and type II diabetes, publicly available summary statistics were used because UK Biobank has limited power for these traits.
source: Because UKBB has limited power for breast cancer, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and type II diabetes, we used publicly available summary statistics.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using external GWAS data.

claim: COJO can condition summary statistics on selected variants by using an LD reference panel.
source: The Conditional and Joint Analysis (COJO) (Yang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2012) program can condition summary statistics on selected variants—in our case, coding variants—by using an LD reference panel.
evidence: This describes the methodology for conditional analysis, supported by citations.

claim: TOPMed subjects of European ancestry were used as an LD reference panel for COJO.
source: For this reference, we used TOPMed subjects of European ancestry (Taliun et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the reference panel used, supported by citation.

claim: eQTL summary statistics were taken from GTEx v7.
source: eQTL summary statistics were taken from GTEx v7.
evidence: This describes the data source for eQTL analysis.

claim: Using the Benjamini-Hochberg method with appropriate correction, 204 out of 220 genes (93%) displayed an eQTL.
source: With this method, 204/220 (93%) of our genes displayed an eQTL, including 134/147 genes with a nearby GWAS peak (91%).
evidence: This is directly supported by the eQTL detection analysis using adjusted FDR.

claim: Using GTEx project FDR statistics, 107 out of 220 genes (49%) had an eQTL at Q < 0.05.
source: Even using the FDR statistics of the GTEx project—which are based on the assumption of testing every gene in every tissue—107/220 (49%) of our genes and 76/147 (52%) of genes near GWAS peaks had an eQTL at Q < 0.05.
evidence: This is directly supported by the eQTL detection analysis using GTEx FDR.

claim: JLIM was run using GWAS summary statistics and GTEx v7 genotypes and phenotypes for trait-relevant tissues.
source: JLIM (Chun et al., 2017) was run using GWAS summary statistics and GTEx v7 genotypes and phenotypes for the tissues listed in Table 2.
evidence: This describes the methodology for colocalization analysis.

claim: Coloc was run using GWAS and GTEx v7 summary statistics for trait-relevant tissues.
source: Coloc (Giambartolomei et al., 2014) was run using GWAS and GTEx v7 summary statistics for the same tissues.
evidence: This describes the methodology for colocalization analysis.

claim: eCAVIAR was run using GWAS and GTEx v7 summary statistics and a reference dataset of LD from UK Biobank.
source: eCAVIAR (Hormozdiari et al., 2016) was run using GWAS and GTEx v7 summary statistics for these tissues, and a reference dataset of LD from UKBB (Weissbrod et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the methodology for colocalization analysis.

claim: MASH was applied to all GTEx tissues using the mashr R-package.
source: MASH was applied to all GTEx tissues using the mashr R-package (Urbut et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the methodology for MASH analysis.

claim: MASH was restricted to non-brain tissues due to the known tendency of brain and non-brain tissues to cluster separately in expression analysis.
source: We restricted this model to non-brain tissues—which include all of our trait-selected tissues—due to the known tendency of brain and non-brain tissues to cluster separately in expression analysis (Battle et al., 2017; Park et al., 2017; Gamazon et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the rationale for tissue selection in MASH, supported by citations.

claim: For many complex traits, TWAS returns a large number of findings (e.g., >150 for LDL cholesterol and >4800 for height).
source: For many complex traits, TWAS returns a large number of findings (e.g., >150 for LDL cholesterol and >4800 for height).
evidence: This is based on the TWAS analysis results.

claim: Most TWAS hits are found in tissues without clear relevance to the trait.
source: Most hits are found in tissues without any clear relevance to the trait and absent in relevant tissues—LDL, for example, has more TWAS associations between expression and eQTL in prostate adenocarcinoma (24 genes associated), brain prefrontal cortex (23 genes associated), and transformed fibroblasts (21 genes associated) than it does in adipose (16 genes associated), blood (11 genes associated), or liver (5 genes associated).
evidence: This is based on the TWAS analysis results showing tissue distribution of hits.

claim: Individual genes identified by TWAS often show inconsistent direction of effect across tissues.
source: Individual genes were often identified as hits in multiple tissues, but with an inconsistent direction of effect—that is, increased gene expression correlated with an increase in the quantitative trait or disease risk in some tissues, but a decrease in others
evidence: This is based on the TWAS analysis results.

claim: GWAS variants were fine-mapped using the SuSiE algorithm.
source: We fine-mapped the GWAS variants located within ±100 kb of our putatively causative genes by applying the SuSiE algorithm (Wang et al., 2020b)
evidence: This describes the methodology for fine-mapping, supported by citation.

claim: An LD reference panel from UK Biobank subjects of European ancestry was used for fine-mapping analysis.
source: An LD reference panel from UKBB subjects of European ancestry was used for this analysis.
evidence: This describes the reference panel used for fine-mapping.

claim: Fine-mapped variants were projected onto active regions of the genome identified using histone modification features, DHS, and ChromHMM enhancers.
source: We projected fine-mapped GWAS variants onto active regions of the genome, identified using three alternative approaches: (i) histone modification features, (ii) DHS, and (iii) ChromHMM enhancers.
evidence: This describes the methodology for functional genomic annotation.

claim: Imputed narrowPeak sets for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 were downloaded from the Roadmap Epigenomics Project for 14 different tissue types.
source: We downloaded imputed narrowPeak sets for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 from the Roadmap Epigenomics Project (Wainberg et al., 2019) ftp site (available here) for 14 different tissue types (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the data sources for histone modification analysis.

claim: The mean activity of a feature was calculated by taking the geometric mean of the corresponding peak strengths from H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 marks.
source: The mean activity/strength of a feature (AF) was calculated by taking the geometric mean of the corresponding peak strengths from H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 marks.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating feature activity.

claim: Activity-by-distance scores were computed for gene-feature pairs by combining activity measurements with linear distances between features and transcription start sites.
source: We then combined these activity measurements with the linear distances between the features and the transcription start sites of causative genes to compute ABD scores (a simplified version of ABC scores Barbeira et al., 2018) for gene–feature pairs
evidence: This describes the methodology for computing ABD scores, with reference to ABC scores.

claim: A high ABD score may serve as a proxy for increased specificity between a chromatin feature and the gene of interest.
source: A high ABD score may serve as a proxy for an increased specificity between a chromatin feature and the gene of interest.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of ABD scores.

claim: The DHS index was downloaded from https://www.meuleman.org/research/dhsindex/.
source: We downloaded the index of human DHS along with biosample metadata from https://www.meuleman.org/research/dhsindex/.
evidence: This describes the data source for DHS analysis.

claim: The DHS index coordinates were converted from hg38 to hg19 using hgLiftOver.
source: The index was in hg38 coordinates, which were converted to hg19 coordinates using the online version of the hgLiftOver package (https://genome.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgLiftOver).
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Tissue-specific chromHMM annotations were downloaded from the Roadmap Epigenomics Project.
source: Tissue-specific chromHMM annotations were downloaded from the Roadmap Epigenomics Project Wainberg et al., 2019 ftp site (available here).
evidence: This describes the data source for ChromHMM analysis.

claim: A fine-mapped variant was considered to fall in an enhancer region if it was housed within a chromHMM segment described as enhancer, bivalent enhancer, or genic enhancer.
source: We considered a fine-mapped variant to fall in an enhancer region if it was housed within a chromHMM segment described as either enhancer, or bivalent enhancer, or genic enhancer.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying variants in enhancer regions.
